summary: Specifies the frame format for encapsulating an IPv6 datagram in a MAPOS frame, and how an IPv6 interface identifier is formed on such links. MAPOS is a link-layer protocol for multiple access over SONET/SDH. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: MAPOS is a fast way for several computers to share an optical fiber line. This memo says how to put IPv6 messages into its packages and how a device works out its address.

questions: how is ipv6 carried over mapos
what is the mapos mtu for ipv6
how are ipv6 interface identifiers formed on mapos
subtitle: How IPv6 packets are framed, addressed and discovered on MAPOS SONET/SDH links.

tldr.problem: IPv6 needs rules for running over MAPOS, a high-speed link-layer protocol with switch-assigned addresses.
tldr.mechanism: IPv6 datagrams go into MAPOS frames with protocol value 0x0057, multicast maps onto the HDLC address, interface identifiers avoid MAPOS addresses, and the Neighbor Discovery link-layer address option is zero-padded to 8 octets.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC that is not a product of an IETF working group, and it has been updated by RFC 8064.

today: RFC 3572 is an Informational RFC that has been updated by RFC 8064. It was not produced by an IETF working group.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
MAPOS (Multiple Access Protocol over SONET/SDH) is a high-speed link-layer protocol. Its frame format is based on HDLC-like framing for PPP, and a Frame Switch connects multiple nodes in a star topology to form a LAN that can span a wide area over long-haul SONET/SDH links.

The RFC covers four things: the frame format for IPv6, the way interface identifiers are formed, duplicate address detection, and the Source/Target Link-layer Address option used in Neighbor Discovery messages. It covers both MAPOS version 1 and MAPOS 16. The IESG note states that it is not a product of an IETF working group and not a standards-track document.
sections.plainLanguage: MAPOS is like a shared hallway in which a central switchboard connects many rooms. This memo teaches IPv6 how to talk down that hallway.

sections.title: Frame Format and MTU
sections.content:
MAPOS uses the same HDLC-like framing as PPP-over-SONET. A frame begins and ends with the flag 01111110 (0x7E) and has address, control and protocol fields. In MAPOS 16 the address field is 16 bits and the control field is omitted. The frame check sequence is 16 bits by default, with an optional 32-bit FCS.

For IPv6 the protocol field must be 0x0057. The information field holds the IPv6 header followed immediately by the payload.

The information field must not exceed 65,280 octets, which is also the default MTU. A Router Advertisement MTU option or manual configuration may lower it. An advertised MTU larger than 65,280, or larger than a configured value, may be logged but must otherwise be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: An IPv6 packet rides inside an envelope marked with a special label, 0x0057, so the receiver knows what is inside. The envelope has a maximum size.

sections.title: Destination Address Mapping
sections.content:
For unicast, the address field holds the HDLC address that the Node Switch Protocol (NSP) assigned to the destination interface. The sender finds it using Neighbor Discovery link-layer address resolution. Address resolution is never performed on IPv6 multicast addresses.

For multicast in MAPOS version 1, the 8-bit address field has its most significant bit set to 1 (multicast) and its least significant bit set to 1 (the end-of-address bit). The other six bits carry the lowest-order six bits of the IPv6 multicast address. If those six bits are all zeros or all ones, they become 111110, making the field 0xFD.

In MAPOS 16, the 16-bit field has the first octet's MSB set to 1, the first octet's LSB set to 0 and the second octet's LSB set to 1. The other 13 bits carry the lowest-order 13 bits of the multicast address. If those are all zeros or all ones, the field is 0xFEFD.
sections.plainLanguage: For one friend, you use the friend's room number. For a group message, the room number is made from the last few digits of the group's address.

sections.title: Interface Identifiers and Duplicate Detection
sections.content:
A node with MAPOS interfaces must create EUI-64 based interface identifiers, and must not derive them from MAPOS addresses. A MAPOS address depends on the frame switch and port, is only unique within a multi-switch environment, can change on a hot-swappable link without a restart, and is the same on both ends of a point-to-point link (0x03 for version 1, 0x0003 for MAPOS 16).

Methods in order of preference: use an IEEE global identifier (EUI-48 or EUI-64) if one is available anywhere on the node, inverting the universal/local bit and inserting 0xFF and 0xFE in the middle of an EUI-48. Otherwise use another source of uniqueness such as a machine serial number, with the u bit set to 0. If nothing good exists, use a random number, also with the u bit 0.

Because the MAPOS address is not assigned until NSP delivers it, a node must run duplicate address detection on all unicast addresses of MAPOS interfaces after that assignment completes.
sections.plainLanguage: Your name tag should not come from your seat number, because seats change. So the tag is built from something that belongs to you, like a serial number, or at worst a random pick.

sections.title: The Link-Layer Address Option
sections.content:
Neighbor Discovery measures the Source/Target Link-layer Address option in units of 8 octets, but a MAPOS address is only 1 octet (version 1) or 2 octets (MAPOS 16). The exact form would give a total of 3 or 4 octets, shorter than 8.

So the address field must be extended with zeros to make the option 8 octets, and the Length field is set to 1. Type is 1 for a source and 2 for a target link-layer address.
sections.plainLanguage: The form has a box that is 8 spaces long, but the address is much shorter. So the rest of the box is filled with zeros.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
MAPOS has no link-layer security. Because a frame switch assigns the address from its switch number and port number, the address indicates where an interface is. If addresses are administered, other nodes cannot easily receive traffic meant for others. Even a node spoofing an IPv6 address in Neighbor Discovery must advertise its true MAPOS address, which makes it easy to locate.

A MAPOS frame carries no sender address, so a node sending improper traffic is hard to identify. The RFC suggests keeping multi-switch environments small, separating them with IP routers, and filtering at boundary routers on IP layer information. It also notes that there is currently no protection against duplication of interface identifiers through accident or forgery.
sections.plainLanguage: The switchboard knows which room each number belongs to, so cheaters are easy to find. But a letter has no return address, so a troublemaker can be hard to trace.
